title: Creating interleaved maths worksheets for my (very lucky) 6 year old
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton wants his Year 2 son to practise maths on paper rather than on screens, and borrows an idea from Dylan Kane for interleaved times-table worksheets. He builds a custom Gemini Gem that writes a daily 20-question sheet in LaTeX, with odd questions on the day's new theme and even questions drawn from a growing pool of earlier themes. He lists the pool, a sequence of 60 themes ordered by difficulty, and the formatting rules he gave the model. Each sheet then takes about twenty seconds to generate. He asks whether this beats writing sheets himself, and admits it does not improve quality but does save time. The prompt takes effort and several rounds of refinement, though he finds that most problems trace back to unclear instructions. The same prompt could be adapted to other ages as weekly low-stakes quizzes.
points: Interleaving can be built into a worksheet by alternating questions on today's concept with questions sampled from an expanding pool of past concepts.
A saved Gemini Gem turns a one-off prompt into a repeatable tool that produces a fresh worksheet in about twenty seconds.
Barton tests AI use against two questions, whether it saves time and whether it makes him do the job better, and here only the first is clearly met.
Most disappointing early outputs trace to vagueness in the prompt, so refining it is itself a clarifying exercise.
The design is portable: swap the pool and theme lists to fit any year group.
quotes: Dylan has created these worksheets so that the odd-numbered questions focus on one times table (the 3s, in the example above), while the even-numbered questions are a mixture of times tables that students have encountered in previous worksheets. This taps into the power of interleaving - one of the Bjork’s desirable difficulties - which has been shown time and time again to improve retention.

The Pool of each new day’s worksheet should include the themes from previous days, so children can practice the things they have learned in the past. Therefore, the Pool should grow by one with the creation of each worksheet
I have two questions when I consider using AI for a task: Does it save me time? Does it help me to do my job better?
Are these worksheets better than I could produce on my own? Not really. Questions on these topics are not hard to write.
The prompt took a while to write. As anyone who has tried this kind of thing can attest, the initial results are never quite what you intended, and several rounds of back-and-forths ensue.

Of course, you can use this prompt yourself with whatever age group of students you teach. Just change the Pool and Theme topics, and you are good to go. They would make nice weekly Low-Stakes Quizzes.
